title: CoCoI: Distributed Coded Inference for Straggler Mitigation
takeaway: Full text: CoCoI splits CNN convolution layers across edge devices with MDS codes so the master decodes after any k of n workers finish. Up to 34.2% lower latency than uncoded under device failure (Scenario 2, Fig 6), 26.5% in Scenario 3, up to 20.2% under straggling (sec V-C); approximate vs optimal split gap <3.3% (Table I); coding overhead 2-9% of layer latency (sec V-A); Proposition 2 guarantees gains when R<=1 and n>=10. Setup: 1 master + 10 Raspberry Pi 4B over WiFi, PyTorch-CPU, VGG16/ResNet18 224x224x3, 20 runs. Limits: reliable master, non-convex objective, only type-1 conv layers, one testbed's shift-exponential fits. The coded-computation mechanism is specific to linear convolutions; webular's first-k-of-n sources are plain replicated requests, for which the paper gives no evidence.
evidence: Fig 6/sec V-C: up to 34.2% lower latency under device failure (coded VGG16/ResNet18 on 10 Raspberry Pis)

title: Latency Guarantees for Caching with Delayed Hits
takeaway: Full text: proves LRU is O(kZ)-competitive for caching with delayed hits (Thm 7, LRU <= 8kZ x OPT; Lemmas 8-9); matches the Theta(Zk) deterministic lower bound from prior work. Experiments: 18 traces (13 industry, 5 Zipf), T=5000 requests, Z up to 100, k up to 30; empirical LRU/OPT ratios stay well below the bound (Figs 2-3). Limits: unit-size pages, fixed cache, no bypass, small traces. It is a worst-case guarantee for an existing policy, so it suggests no design change to webular's in-flight coalescing and its assumptions (uniform size, no bypass) do not match fetched web content.
evidence: Thm 7 (sec 3): LRU <= 8kZ x OPT; sec 4: empirical ratios far below bound on 18 traces

title: Preference Leakage
takeaway: Full text (first ~100k chars): preference leakage when the data generator and judge are related. Mistral-7B SFT on GPT-4o vs Gemini-1.5 data gives preference leakage score 23.6% (28.7% Arena-Hard, 18.4% AlpacaEval 2.0) while GPT-4o vs LLaMA-3.3 gives ~0 (Table 1); inheritance 19.3-22.3%, same family 8.9%, different series 2.8% (Table 2); SFT 23.6%, DPO 5.2%, ICL -2.7% (Table 3); judges recognize their own students' outputs near chance (41-53%) vs BERT classifier 82.4% (Table 5); contextual calibration cut Error Bias 17.8 to 7.3 (Table 7). Setup: GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5, LLaMA-3.3-70B, 30k UltraFeedback prompts. Limits: few judges, small case study. The bias is for judges related to a model that trained on the judged data; for webular's agent tests the sound reading is 'avoid judge and judged output from the same family', with the SFT-specific magnitudes not applying to prompt-only agents.
evidence: Table 1: PLS 23.6% (GPT-4o vs Gemini-1.5 data) vs ~0 for unrelated; Table 2: same family 8.9%, different series 2.8%

title: A Scalable Crawling Algorithm Utilizing Noisy Change-Indicating Signals

GREEDY-NCIS (handles false positives) beats GREEDY and GREEDY-CIS in nearly all cases (sec 6.6, Fig 6); approximations match exact only when bandwidth m <= 500. Setup: Poisson simulations on the 18.5M-URL Kolobov 2019 set, R=100, up to 10,000 pages, 100 reps. Limits: Poisson/i.i.d. assumptions, partial parameter estimation, delay handling heuristic. Supports treating sitemap lastmod/ETag as noisy hints with learned precision/recall rather than trusting them; a scheduling component, not extraction.
evidence: Sec 2/Fig 1: sitemap precision <0.2, recall <0.5; sec 6.6: GREEDY-NCIS beats GREEDY with false positives

title: Proximity: Approximate Caching for RAG
takeaway: Proximity: Rust cache (Python bindings) reusing retrieval results for near-duplicate query embeddings with tolerance tau. MMLU (wiki_dpr, FAISS-HNSW) and MedRAG (PubMed, FAISS-Flat), LLaMA 3.1; MedRAG-Zipf LSH: -77.2% database calls, -72.5% latency (abstract, sec 1); hit rate up to 93-98.4% at tau>=5 (sec 4.3.3); accuracy 85.8% to 84.1% as tau 2.5 to 10, MedRAG accuracy 37% at tau=10 (sec 4.3.1); LSH lookup 4.8 microseconds vs FLAT 13 ms at 200k entries. Tau set manually, advantage needs skewed workloads. It caches by embedding similarity over a vector index; webular cache.ts keys fetched pages/results, and near-duplicate-query reuse for web search would need an embedding step that costs more than the cached call saves.
evidence: Sec 4.3.1: accuracy collapses to 37% at tau=10 on MedRAG; -77.2% DB calls on Zipf-skewed vector retrieval only

title: Search Wisely: Mitigating Sub-optimal Agentic Searches By Reducing Uncertainty

The fix is an RL reward (beta-GRPO, gating on minimum token probability of the search query, beta 0.4): avg EM 0.344 vs 0.309 (Table 2, ~3.5 points, abstract says 4%), over-search 21.10% to 19.89%, under-search 42.04% to 34.71% (sec 5). Setup: Qwen2.5-3B, NQ+HotpotQA training, seven QA benchmarks, Wikipedia 2018 + E5, 2 A100s. Limits: 3B only. It needs token log-probs and RL training; a prompt rule 'search whenever not certain' is an extrapolation the paper never tests, so it is not evidence for server.ts instructions.

title: Search-Time Data Contamination
takeaway: Search-time contamination (STC): Perplexity Sonar Pro / Reasoning Pro / Deep Research on HLE, SimpleQA, GPQA, queries run May 15-Jun 15 2025. About 3.4% of HLE items had a HuggingFace page with the answer (84/2,500 Sonar Pro; Table 1, sec 3.1); SimpleQA <1.2%, GPQA 1.90-4.15%. Contaminated HLE items scored >10 points higher (Sonar Pro) and ~20 points higher (Deep Research); SimpleQA 100% on contaminated items; blocking HF cut accuracy ~15% on contaminated questions (Fig 4). Limits: narrow URL-substring detector (huggingface + benchmark name), mostly one vendor, preliminary. Applies to any search-enabled eval whose test set is mirrored online: log retrieved URLs, block HF/benchmark mirrors, apply date cutoffs.

title: MetaRAG: Metamorphic Testing for Hallucination Detection in RAG
takeaway: Full text: MetaRAG splits a RAG answer into factoids, makes synonym (should stay supported) and antonym (should be contradicted) variants, asks an LLM whether the retrieved context supports each, and scores the response by the worst factoid (sec 3). Best F1 0.939 (precision 1.000, recall 0.885, Table 2), config 16 most stable F1 0.940 +/- 0.012 over five seeds (Table 3); about 2.3 s and 29k tokens per run (Table 4). Setup: 23 proprietary enterprise docs, 67 labeled responses (36 faithful, 31 hallucinated), GPT-4.1 family; authors implemented it in TypeScript (App D). Limits: one private dataset, tiny labeled set tuned at tau 0.5, class-balancing edits to responses, many LLM calls per answer, ~572-token median context vs noisier long web pages; Table 2/4 swap precision and recall for config 5.
evidence: Table 2: F1 0.939 (P 1.000, R 0.885) on only 67 responses; Table 4: 29k tokens per run

title: Rethinking HTTP API Rate Limiting: A Client-Side Approach
takeaway: Client-side token-bucket rate limiting (WB/ATB/AATB) emulated in Python 3.13 asyncio with Envoy 1.33 rate limiter (capacity 100, refill 80/min), real search-log trace (800 requests) and synthetic 5 and 100 clients. Versus exponential backoff: 429s -62.7% (WB), -70.1% (ATB), -93.2% (AATB) with +25.5%/+21.3%/+27.6% longer duration (Fig 1a-c); at 100 clients and 800 requests WB only -19.3% (Fig 1g-i); AATB needs shared telemetry (1,106 update messages). Emulation only, no production. Token-bucket logic ports to TypeScript; fewer 429s costs 20-30% more duration, which matters for src/core/http.ts. The adaptive variant needs telemetry webular lacks.
evidence: Fig 1a-c: 429s -70.13% ATB, +21.26% duration vs exponential backoff (800-request trace)

title: Is Misinformation More Open? robots.txt Gatekeeping on the Web

Avg ASR 40.35% (Table 3); Out-of-Scope Parameter highest 76.5%; DeepSeek-V3.1 60.94% vs GPT-5 37.17%; stronger tool-callers more vulnerable (sec 6.2). Only defense tested, MCIP, cuts avg ASR 40.35% to 28.69% (Table 4) - so framing alone does not eliminate attack. Retrieval Injection (sec 4.4) is the web-extraction relevant class. Limits: two file-system MCP servers only; intro and tables disagree on counts. Holds for webular: mark fetched content untrusted, but expect partial mitigation (about 30% relative drop) not a fix.

title: Diversification as Risk Minimization
takeaway: Full text: VRisker greedy risk-minimizing diversification over user intents. Abstract: up to 33% fewer worst-case intent failures at 2% average cost (INTENT-2, k=25, Sec 6.2 Fig 4); (1-1/e)=63% guarantee for modular metrics (Thm 2), loose bound ~0.15/0.09/0.05 for nDCG at k=5/10/20 (Thm 3); beta=0.05 gives 20-30% less worst-case loss for 3-5% cost (Fig 3); 7.84 ms/query at 71,933 candidates. Setup: NTCIR INTENT-2 (95 queries), TREC Web 2012 (50 queries, uniform intents), MovieLens. Limits: needs intent probabilities and per-intent relevance, mutually exclusive intents, beta and target level chosen by hand, single-query. The 'one result per host' heuristic is not from the paper; only usable if webular can estimate query intents.
evidence: Sec 6.2 Fig 4: 33% worst-case risk cut for 2% cost on INTENT-2 k=25; Thm 2: >=63% of optimal

title: ARC: Cache Mechanism for Agent RAG

It caches embedding-space neighbors of a local vector index; webular's cache.ts holds fetched pages/results keyed by URL or query, which has no vector hubness signal, so the mechanism does not map.

title: Enhancing reliability in AI inference services: empirical study of production incidents
takeaway: Full text: Microsoft analysis of 156 severity-2/2.5 LLM inference incidents (Apr-Jun 2025), kappa 0.89 on labeling (sec 3.3). Inference engine failures ~60% (94/156), timeouts ~40% of those; infrastructure ~20%, configuration ~16%, operational ~4% (Table 4); 74% auto-detected, 48% 'monitor only' (Sec 5.1, Table 5); connection-liveness fix cut one customer's HTTP 408 rate 2.72% to 0.47% (sec 5.2, Fig 7, directional, single customer). Limits: high-severity only, one platform, manual labels, no raw data. These are server-side GPU incidents; the timeout, 429, config validation and health-probe lessons plausibly transfer to a client's per-host isolation, the GPU/KV-cache ones do not.
evidence: Table 4: engine failures 94/156 (~60%), timeouts ~40% of them; sec 5.2: 408 rate 2.72% to 0.47% (one customer)

title: Performance of MCP-Enabled LLM Agents
takeaway: Cline 3.14.0 as MCP host via OpenRouter, 9 LLMs, 3 MCP servers (Time, Playwright, Google Maps), 8 tasks, 820 completed tasks, plus a 90-day OpenRouter trace. No direct-tool baseline, snapshot as of May 2025, table inconsistencies. Supports keeping webular's MCP tool list and descriptions small (token cost scales with tool count), but gives no server-language or quality result.

title: Decentralized RAG with Source Reliabilities Secured on Blockchain

title: Stochasticity in Agentic Evaluations: Quantifying Inconsistency with Intraclass Correlation
takeaway: Full text: ICC(1,1) of repeated agent runs on GAIA and FRAMES, 64 trials/question, o4-mini judge. Table 2 (GAIA): GPT-4o -> GPT-5 search L1 ICC 0.561 -> 0.774, L2 0.662 -> 0.745, L3 0.304 -> 0.629 (L3 accuracy 6.6% -> 44.2%); Table 3 (FRAMES n=50): GPT-5 77.31% acc but ICC 0.496 vs GPT-4o 63.54% / 0.735; o4-mini deep research ICC 0.664 (FRAMES), 0.621 (GAIA). Convergence: Levels 1-2 stabilize by ~8-16 trials, Level 3 by ~32 (matches takeaway); Eq 9-10: at sigma_b^2/sigma_w^2 ~ 5, B=400, n=100 tasks x T=4 trials gives 68% lower SE than n=10 x T=40. Limits: binary scoring, judge not validated for consistency, ICC(1,1) only, FRAMES subset of 50 of 824, mostly OpenAI models. Method is language-agnostic; webular's own variance sources (page drift, rate limits) are unmeasured.
evidence: Table 3: GPT-5 FRAMES 77.31% acc with ICC 0.496 vs GPT-4o 63.54% / 0.735; ICC stabilizes by 8-16 trials (32 for L3)

title: When Do Tools and Planning Help? Cost/Latency Benchmark
takeaway: Planner-Executor-Replanner (LangGraph, Python) vs one-shot, GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini, 60 examples per dataset (splits of 20), Event-QA and CMV. Event-QA: GPT-4o with DBpedia tools 67.5% at ~317 s vs 47.5% at ~8 s NoPlanning; mini with Wikipedia 55% at ~84 s vs 35% at ~7 s (Table II). CMV: planning hurts, GPT-4o NoPlanning 70% at ~6 s vs PlanningSearch 40% at 21-27 s; mini NoPlanning 75% vs 50% at 150-216 s (Table III). Small n, two OpenAI models, final numbers average a split also used for tuning. Planning/tools help knowledge-grounded questions at 10-40x latency and hurt on argument tasks, so agent task sets should include both kinds and report latency/cost.

title: Don't Break the Cache
takeaway: Prompt caching on DeepResearch Bench with Deep Agents, 40 sessions per condition, 10K-token system prompt. Cost reduction: GPT-5.2 79.6% (exclude tool results), Claude Sonnet 4.5 78.5% (system prompt only), GPT-4o 45.9%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 41.4% (Table 1); TTFT gain GPT-4o 30.9%, Claude 22.9%, GPT-5.2 13.0%, Gemini 6.1%; full-context caching regressed TTFT for GPT-4o (-8.8%) (Table 2). Savings grow with prompt size (54-89% at 50K tokens); no benefit below caching minimum (500 tokens). Limits: n=40, one benchmark, Jan-2026 pricing, abstract range 41-80% mismatches Table 2 Gemini 28-41%. Holds: keep static tool descriptions first and stable, dynamic tool results out of the cached prefix.

title: Key Collision Attack on LLM Semantic Caching
takeaway: CacheAttack: key-collision attacks on SEMANTIC (embedding-similarity) LLM caches (GPTCache tau=0.8, Qwen3-8B, 4,185 SC-IPI prompts, 1,000-step budget). Hit rate 86.9% semantic cache, 85.8% semantic KV cache vs GA baseline 36.2%/34.0% (Table 1); AWS Bedrock 80.6%, Azure 88.3% (Table 2); agent hit rate 90.6% (Table 3); cross-model transfer as low as 49.8% (Table 4); salting cuts hit rate up to 21.0 points (Table 5). Limits: 50 benign queries, attack slow/detectable. The attack targets embedding-similarity keys; webular's cache.ts uses exact keys only, which is the paper's implied safe design, so the item is already satisfied (keep exact keys, add no semantic key layer).
evidence: Table 1: 86.9% hijack on semantic cache; exact-key cache not attackable by this method

title: Re-TRAC
takeaway: Re-TRAC compresses each trajectory into a structured state and prepends it to the next round (default 8). BrowseComp300: o3 54.9 to 69.8 at RT@8, beats majority vote 64.3 and best-of-8 68.0 (Table 3); 30B-A3B model reaches 53.0 BrowseComp, 78.2 GAIA (Table 2); claims ~50% of resources of other test-time scaling (Sec 5.2). Small models need SFT on 33K synthetic QA (4B: 2.7 to 30.0, Table 4), and weak self-summarization limits 4B (Table 6); models can get stuck on one path (needs free-use prompt). Frontier-model use is training-free and language-independent, so the state-handoff loop ports to agent.ts, but gains were on BrowseComp-style hard search and cost grows per round.

title: Illusory completion in search agents (Epistemic Ledger)

LiveLedger (fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B tracking per-constraint state, state table injected each turn) raises accuracy 4.4-16.1 pts and cuts UAR 6.2-16.7 pts across six agents, e.g. DeepSeek-V4 43.6 to 59.7 (Table 2); tracker adds 1.1-8.4% latency, evaluator about $0.065-0.108 per question. 484 questions with independent constraints only, Serper+Jina, LLM evaluator (91% human agreement, kappa 0.76). A per-constraint ledger in research.ts fits, but chained multi-hop questions were not tested.

title: When Handshakes Tell the Truth: Bad Bots via JA4 TLS Fingerprints
takeaway: JA4 classifier on JA4DB (227,404 records, 39,080-record test): XGBoost F1 0.9732, accuracy 0.9862, AUC 0.998 (body reports AUC only for XGBoost, abstract credits CatBoost); labels from a keyword heuristic ('bot' in application field), not verified; adversarial robustness untested. Agent generators had significantly higher coverage on 4 of 7 benchmarks (sec 4.2, Fig 5) but BCEL was 54% below the human baseline; coverage guidance helped human generators ~40% but was not significant for agent generators (Finding 2); predicate feedback improved coverage in 74% of runs yet final coverage was similar; median 32% slowdown (Table 2). Limits: Java/JQF only, one model, branch coverage proxy, possible pretraining exposure, abstract says seven benchmarks but sec 4.1.2 lists six. Tooling does not transfer to TypeScript; evidence for structured-input generators in a web-parser fuzz test is indirect.
evidence: Sec 4.2/Fig 5: agent generators higher on 4 of 7 Java targets, BCEL 54% below human; Table 2: median 32% slower

title: Reasoning Trace Inversion for Abstention in LLMs
takeaway: Full text (first ~100k chars): Trace Inversion reconstructs the query from the answer trace and flags a wrong-question answer by similarity; it has the best Abstain Accuracy in 33 of 36 model-dataset settings (Table 1, sec 5.2), +8.7% average over the strongest baseline (phi-4 +11.6%, Qwen2.5-32B +9.5%); on datasets with unanswerable queries accuracy drops 3-7 points vs ~13-20 for baselines (Table 2); individual distance modules 68.6-70.4%, majority-vote ensemble 73.2% (Table 3); chain-of-thought prompting lowers baseline abstention ~2.6% (Table 4). Setup: phi-4, Qwen2.5-32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, gpt-oss-120b; nine QA datasets, 3 seeds, temp 0.1. Limits: 3+ LLM calls per query, designed for reasoning models, QA abstention only, ensemble needs a sentence-embedding model and Granite Guardian. Prompt-based, so API-portable, but the extra calls are a real cost for webular's answer workflow.
evidence: Table 1: best Abstain Accuracy in 33 of 36 settings, +8.7% avg over strongest baseline; needs 3+ LLM calls

title: I-CALM: Confidence-Aware Abstention for LLM Hallucination Mitigation
takeaway: Full text (I-CALM): prompt-only, black-box; verbal confidence + announced payoffs (+1 correct, -1 wrong, +0.4 abstain) + five norms, scored with a two-stage protocol (answer-or-abstain, then forced guess) that separates targeted abstention from blanket refusal. J_abs +28.7% over strongest coverage-matched baseline on PopQA (3 models, Sec 3.2); highest J_abs in 14 of 15 model-dataset settings and lower false-answer rate than Scheme A in 14 (Sec 4.2). Ablation (Table 3, GPT-5 mini): full coverage 0.56, FAR 0.36, J_abs 0.44; no confidence -> coverage 0.25, J_abs 0.30; no payoffs -> 0.76/0.33. Explicit IDK collapses coverage (0.29 GPT-5 mini, 0.002 Llama). Limits: short single-answer factual QA only; does not fix knowledge gaps (SimpleQA-Verified); verbal confidence is a practical signal. The two-stage eval design transfers to webular's report; multi-field extraction and missing ground truth are untested.
evidence: Sec 4.2: highest J_abs in 14 of 15 settings; Table 3: no confidence -> coverage 0.25 vs 0.56

title: TRUSTDESC: Preventing Tool Poisoning via Trusted Description Generation

Relevant to web-schemas.ts as description hardening, but generation requires running the tools and the gain is modest (+2 to +3.6 pts).

takeaway: Full text read only through ~100k of 198k chars. Only relevant if act accepts mid-run revisions and tools have real compensations; benefit shown is less waste, not better answers.

title: Agreement Metrics for LLM-as-Judge Evaluation: What to Report and Why
takeaway: Full text (first ~100k chars): on binary verdicts Pearson r, Spearman rho, Kendall tau-b, phi and MCC are the same statistic (sec 4.1, Fact 1); kappa = q x phi with q in (0,1] (Eq. 8); self-preference case: accuracy 0.880 vs 0.876 always-positive baseline (McNemar p=0.549) while kappa 0.402 (sec 4.4). Abstention makes full-set accuracy identified only to an interval of width equal to the uncovered fraction; cascade gamma=0.612 gives [0.534, 0.923] (sec 5.2/5.4, Eq. 10); handling rules give accuracy 0.647/0.580/0.548 (Table 5); across 24 protocols on 2,007 decisions accuracy spans 0.551-0.899 (34.8 points) while kappa ranges -0.067 to 0.068 (sec 5.5); micro-kappa 0.040 vs macro 0.009 (sec 6). Reanalysis of 24 coded papers and three published evaluations, no new experiments. Limits: binary verdicts, asymptotic variance, one judge/domain. 2x2-count statistics port easily to agreement.ts.
evidence: Sec 5.5: accuracy spans 0.551-0.899 across 24 protocols on 2,007 decisions; sec 4.4: acc 0.880 vs 0.876 baseline, kappa 0.402

title: On Effectiveness and Efficiency of Agentic Tool-calling and RL Training

Setup: Qwen2.5-3B / Qwen3-4B GRPO in VERL; Amazon authors. Supports storing seed, system prompt, template and history policy per bench row; RL parts irrelevant.

title: BAGEN: Are LLM Agents Budget-Aware?
takeaway: BAGEN: do agents estimate remaining budget? 5 models (GPT-5.2, Opus 4.7, Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3-235B) x 4 environments (Sokoban, Search-R1, SWE-bench, Warehouse), 128 rollouts per model. Task success vs feasibility prediction r~0.35 (Table 1); all 20 pairs underestimate remaining budget (Sec 5.2); models still predict feasibility >70% after 60% of budget on failed runs (Sec 5.4). Stopping on 'impossible' predictions saves 28-64% tokens on failed rollouts at 1.6-4.2 pp success cost, false aborts 2.2-6.6% (Table 3, Sec 6.1). SFT lifts a 7B model's feasibility accuracy 25.5% to ~90% (not usable for hosted models). Supports enforcing budgets in the MCP layer instead of trusting agent self-estimates; the early-stop gain costs success.

title: Dr. DocBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Expert-Level and Difficult Document Parsing
takeaway: Full text: Dr. DocBench has 4,514 annotated pages from 312 PDFs (52 BISAC subjects, 14 languages, ~70k annotations), hard pages picked by disagreement among three parsers. Best general VLM GPT-5.5 scores 61.94 (Table 1); MinerU 2.5 best on tables (TEDS 55.85); borderless tables collapse (Doubao TEDS 8.1, Table 4); reading-order error grows with context (0.16 to 0.47, sec 5.1). Limits: one unified prompt, structured formats not covering all domains. Metrics are tool-agnostic, so they could score webular's extraction on PDFs, but it is a PDF/VLM parsing benchmark, a weak fit for an HTML scraping eval set.

title: Self-Healing Agentic Orchestrators for Reliable Tool-Augmented LLM Systems
takeaway: Self-healing orchestrator on 100 synthetic tasks with simulated tools, 7 fault classes, intensity 0-0.5, 3 seeds, 9,000 executions. Success 98.8% vs 94.5% retry-only, 93.8% replanning, 70.1% static (Table 5); at intensity 0.4-0.5, 97.3% vs 86.7% retry-only (Table 6); timeouts 79.3% and unavailable tools 75.3% were its weakest (Table 7); advantage comes from root-cause classification and budgeted recovery, ablation 99.3% to 95.7% (Table 8). Author-built tasks and fault templates may favor the policy; simulated tools, small model-in-the-loop (15 tasks). A Retry-After handler alone equals the retry-only baseline here, so the paper supports classification + targeted recovery, not retry-timing changes.
evidence: Table 5: 98.8% vs 94.5% retry-only on 100 synthetic tasks; Table 8 ablation 99.3% to 95.7%

title: Recuse Signal: Agent Compliance with In-Band Governance
takeaway: Recuse Signal: in-band deny/throttle/warn/halt directives to LLM agents in tool loops. Access-time deny recusal 100% GPT-4o-mini and Claude Sonnet 4.5, 75% GPT-4o, 55% Gemini 2.5 Flash, pooled 82.5% (66/80; Table 3, sec 7); no-signal control completed 98/100. Throttle: no effect (null); warn surfaced to operator 0/100. Mid-task halt: 0/20 stopped in-band for OpenAI models (Table 2); Gemini 16/20, GPT-4o-mini 0/20 (Table 4). Loop-level interceptor stopped 120/120 enforced vs 28/120 cooperative (sec 8.2, mock harness). Limits: small n=20 cells, 4-step SSH task, mock enforcement, cooperative not security. Conclusion supports enforcing signals in code, not relying on the model: for webular's fetch-policy.ts, parse deny fail-closed and enforce deterministically; throttle in code.
evidence: Sec 8.2: interceptor stopped 120/120 vs 28/120 cooperative; Table 3 model recusal 55%-100%

title: Cost-Aware Speculative Execution
takeaway: Decision rule for speculative execution in agent DAGs: speculate if EV = P*L_value - (1-P)*C_spec >= (1-alpha)*C_spec, P from a Beta-Binomial posterior with dependency-type prior (n0=2; data outweighs prior after ~10 observations, sec 7.3). Worked numbers only: critical branching factor k_crit ~5.7 / 3.8 / 2.9 at alpha 1 / 0.5 / 0 (sec 7.6); streaming cancel at 300 of 1,000 tokens cuts waste $0.0165 to $0.0060 (-64%, sec 10.3). Synthetic validation only (Appendix D); no live system, runtime overhead unmeasured. Limits (sec 14): static DAG only, elastic API capacity assumed, priors uncalibrated. Only safe for side-effect-free or staged downstream steps, so for src/commands/act.ts it applies to read-only prefetch, not to state-changing actions.
evidence: Sec 10.3: cancel at 300/1000 tokens cuts waste $0.0165 to $0.0060 (-64%); synthetic validation only (App D)

title: The Coin Flip Judge?
takeaway: Full text: 29 question-response pairs, two OpenAI judges (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini), 50 pairwise and 50 pointwise trials per question. Mean pairwise flip rate ~13.6% (13.3% / 13.9%), 28% of questions >20%, max 56% (Table 1); GPT-4o-mini picked response A as majority winner 72% of the time (p=0.024; Table 2); cross-judge agreement 76%, kappa 0.51 (sec 5.6); temperature 0 cut flips 43-79% but not to zero (Table 4); changing the prompt template changed the majority verdict in 25% of cases (Table 5); ICC(2,1) 0.58-0.77 (Table 7); ~11 trials needed for 95% agreement with the 50-trial verdict on average (Table 6). Limits: one provider, small set of competitive pairs, same-family judging, two templates, no human comparison. Supports repeat judgments plus order randomization in webular's agent tests.
evidence: Table 1: mean pairwise flip rate 13.6% (max 56%); Table 6: ~11 trials for 95% agreement with 50-trial verdict

title: Where Did It Go Wrong? Process-Level Evaluation of Web Agents (WebStep)
takeaway: Full text (WebStep): 1,800 tasks over 10 self-hosted sites each run as a deterministic semantic MDP, so states/transitions are logged for free; 6 agents. Table 2: small agents cluster 34-37% terminal success (UI-TARS +5.9% exploration, -4.7% execution vs GUI-Owl); Claude CUA 85.3%, OpenAI CUA 82.7%. title: Reliability without Validity
takeaway: Full text: 21 judges, MT-Bench/JudgeBench/RewardBench, 118 runs, ~541k judgments. Exact match exceeds Cohen's kappa by 33.8-41.3 pp on MT-Bench (about 24 pp JudgeBench, 10 pp RewardBench; Sec 4.1, Table 2), so raw exact match inflates agreement. Rankings shift up to 14-15 positions across benchmarks (Table 5); high test-retest does not imply validity (Qwen 3 8B test-retest 0.992 with position bias 0.192; Gemini 2.5 Flash 0.988/0.125; Table 3). Proposes a minimum validation protocol (chance-corrected agreement, AB+BA swaps, >=3 replicates, >=2 benchmarks). Limits: English text-only, March-April 2026 snapshot, one pairwise rubric, reasoning suppressed. Holds for any webular LLM judge: report kappa and swap order, validate on in-domain labels.

title: Keeping the Cache Warm Pays: Keepalive Economics
takeaway: Full text: client-side keepalive pings keep a long prompt prefix warm. Holds for webular if idle gaps are long and prefixes are byte-identical; cap the pause length or pinging costs more.

The in-flight dedup is a standard pending-promise map and cheap to check in cache.ts, but this paper does not quantify it for web fetches.

Limits: reliability is not validity; sparse imbalanced design; intro/abstract rollout counts disagree (30,859 vs 29,923). Applies to webular's bench report only if it reports system-level rankings and avoids model-level claims from one scaffold; the framework needs multi-scaffold data webular does not have.

title: Curating Always-Loaded Context for LLM Agents: A Capacitated Assortment Model
takeaway: Formal analysis of always-loaded context files. Any nonnegative-value file has |S| <= Q/rho independent of pool size (Prop 1, sec 3); accretion loses without bound as the file grows (Cor 1); deleting by non-compliance is value-blind (Prop 3); admit after two sightings in a window (Thm 1, sec 4.3). Experiment: pools of 200/800/3,200 from real repository files, Claude Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5.5, 2,880 runs on 60 ManyIFEval tasks: gross value peaks at about 200 loaded instructions for N=3,200 then falls (Haiku 5.0 to 0.6, Sonnet 23.8 to 4.0), optimum 10-40 items (sec 5); IFScale compliance 0.92-1.00 at 10 requirements to 0.067-0.689 at 500. Keyword compliance only, assumptions of monotone dilution, simulated regret. Supports keeping AGENTS.md short and admitting rules by repeated need, not a specific line cap.
evidence: Sec 5: at N=3,200 loaded-value falls (Sonnet 23.8 to 4.0) beyond about 200 loaded instructions; IFScale 500 requirements compliance 0.067-0.689

title: Traceable World State deterministic replay

title: MetaCascade: Attacks on Agent Skills via Metadata-Only Poisoning
takeaway: Full text: MetaCascade poisons only skill metadata. Average ASR 74.24% without defenses (Table 1), 35.53 points above best baseline; 63.33% under four defenses; Retrieval Hit@1 49.75% (Table 3); ASR 60.00-86.06% across agent-LLM pairs (Table 4), 69.72-76.34% across embedders (Table 5). Four skill repos, agents Hermes and OpenClaw, GPT-5.4, metadata cap 1,290 characters, ~121k tokens to craft each attack (Table 7). Supports that metadata drives selection, which makes the SKILL.md description the lever, but it measures attack success, not call-rate improvement from better wording.

title: When Messages Go Wrong: Communication Faults in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
takeaway: 29,000+ runs (18,900 primary matrix) on 100 tasks (WebArena x3, SWE-bench, TheAgentCompany), three AutoGen topologies, three small/open LLMs. 89.4% of applied faults had downstream consequence, 80.2% ended in task failure (Sec 4.2); 20.7% of failures were silent (76.2% for partial-content faults). Flat topology 53.0% success vs 3.3% sequential and 3.2% hierarchical (Sec 4.4); swapping the LLM recovers only 0.2-4.5% of failures vs 19.3-27.0% by switching to Flat. Limits: AutoGen only, no TypeScript, no research-style workflow. Qualitative lessons (redundant evidence paths, validate handoffs, watch partial-content silent failures) plausible for research.ts; numbers do not transfer.
evidence: Sec 4.4: Flat 53.0% vs Sequential 3.3% success; evidence-handoff (I4) fault drives gap

title: Fetch Me If You Can: Analysis of Fetch Metadata
takeaway: Full text: crawl of Tranco top 1M (Jun-Aug 2025, Playwright Firefox): only 2,295 sites (0.23%) deploy Fetch Metadata policies; 2.8% of top 1k; Google+Meta = 92.9% of protected top-1k sites (Sec 7, Table 4). 14,141 protected endpoints; 94% return a different status code on violation, 5.5% change content. Median 2.17% of tested endpoints on protected sites are protected. Browsers attach Sec-Fetch-*; scripts cannot modify them, so non-browser clients like Bun fetch send none (Sec 2.1) and may see differing responses on protected endpoints. Limits: unauthenticated landing-page-seeded crawl, partial coverage. Real but low-prevalence effect (0.23% of sites); worthwhile only as a cheap optional header set, not a priority.
evidence: Sec 7/Table 4: 2,295 of top-1M sites (0.23%) deploy FM policies; 94% change status on violation

Simulated provider guarantees, GPT only, four tasks. Concerns retrying side-effecting tools; webular's src/core/http.ts retries read-only fetches where duplicate effects do not occur, so there is nothing to change.

title: TRAP: Tool-result Replay Attack for Probing Misbinding in LLM Agents
takeaway: TRAP / ReplayBench: tool-result replay across LlamaIndex, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, 8 LLMs, 19 scenarios, n=10 per config. Mean final-state error rate 0.649 on cross-task replay, 38.1% of configs reach 1.0 (Table 1); model identity explains eta^2=0.742 of variance, frameworks barely differ 0.607-0.686 (Tables 4-6); call-ID binding, one-shot tickets and world-state epochs each cut it to 0 (Table 2, only GPT-5.5 + LlamaIndex, two scenarios); object-ID matching fails on same-object duplicate replay. Python frameworks, synthetic sandboxes. Binding every cached/returned result to its call id fits src/core/cache.ts if cache entries could be re-served to a different call; webular's cache keyed by request already binds per call.
evidence: Table 2 (sec 4.3): call-ID binding drives replay FSER to 0 on GPT-5.5/LlamaIndex, two scenarios; Table 1: mean FSER 0.649

title: Why Agentic Workflows Fail: A Taxonomy Derived from Literature and Empirical Data
takeaway: Agentic workflow failure taxonomy (397 literature records, 1,196 GitHub episodes, 229 repos; 65 types, 16 families): GitHub failures concentrate in S3 iterative execution (77.3% vs 30.7% literature) and capability D actuation (65.5% vs 17.4%); S3xD holds 64.8% of GitHub records (Sec V-D); External API/Tool Failure 26.3% vs 2.8% (Table V); human kappa 0.65-0.71 (Table II). A stage-by-capability matrix is a reasonable doctor layout, with no evidence it improves outcomes (listed as future work).

title: BrowseSafe++: Prompt Injection Detection Across Web Contexts and Browser Views
takeaway: BrowseSafe++: 38,675 attack/control page pairs, 4 views (HTML, Markdown, AX tree, screenshot), 16 text models. Fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B guard F1 98.29 HTML, 93.26 Markdown, 92.98 AX tree (FPR 1.35/7.40/5.77%); best prompted F1 ~91.5 with 13-15% FPR. Adaptive attacks raise success from 0.5-4% to 30-95%; the guard only lowers 64-attempt ASR from 93.55% to 84.18% and cuts clean completion 97.85% -> 91.21%. Markdown is attackable and conversion shifts recall by up to 14-16 points, so an untrusted-content label on scrape output holds; a guard is not a defense against adaptive attackers.
evidence: Table 2/sec 4.1: guard F1 93.26 on Markdown, FPR 7.40%; Table 9: ASR 93.55% -> 84.18%

title: Quota-Based Aging for Prediction-Guided Scheduling
takeaway: Quota-based aging (QBA) for LLM token-level batching: synthetic Poisson arrivals, 100 seeds, token budget B=128, KV 8192, plus 100 Azure windows. Mean wait FCFS 0.179 s, PSF 0.123, AA 0.178, QBA 0.146; true-long P99 FCFS 0.766, PSF 2.097, QBA 1.446, AA 0.491 (Table II). QBA keeps ~59% of PSF's mean gain. Needs a binary length predictor (assumed, not evaluated); simulator-only; AA beats QBA on P99 under load. Solves LLM inference batching, not crawl fairness; no evidence for a crawl scheduler. Downgrade to not-applicable.

title: Fresh at Decision, Stale at Action

title: Tremulant: Latency in Serverless Platforms beyond the 99th Percentile
takeaway: Full text: warm-start latency tails on 7 FaaS platforms, 53 days, empty functions, 3 s inter-arrival bursts. At p99.99 warm calls are 6.5x-947.5x slower than platform median vs 3.4x for an EC2 baseline (Fig 1, Sec 5); tail factor of DD 5.85 (p99) -> 138.46 (p99.9) -> 424.05 (p99.99); more than 50% of calls at p99.99 are warm on 5 of 6 platforms (Fig 3); 4 other datasets used for validation (Table 2). Limits: empty functions, p99.99 rests on only 28-192 calls per platform, single-day datasets, attribution to platform overhead is a hypothesis. It supports reporting percentiles beyond p99, but its tail evidence is FaaS-specific; a local mise latency benchmark needs enough samples (>=10x the percentile denominator) rather than these numbers.
applies_to: mise latency benchmark percentiles to p99.9
evidence: Fig 1/Sec 5: warm p99.99 6.5x-947.5x median vs EC2 3.4x; p99.99 rests on 28-192 calls (Sec 4)

title: TRACER: Trajectory-Aware Tool Retrieval
takeaway: Full text: TRACER builds a prefix trie of logged successful trajectories plus embedding similarity and a small logistic blend.
